claim: Mutations within the kinase domain of the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) are common oncogenic driver events in non-small cell lung cancer.
source: Mutations within the kinase domain of the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) are common oncogenic driver events in non-small cell lung cancer.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Activation of EGFR in normal cells is primarily driven by growth-factor-binding-induced dimerization.
source: Although the activation of EGFR in normal cells is primarily driven by growth-factor-binding-induced dimerization, mutations on different exons of the kinase domain of the receptor have been found to affect the equilibrium between its active and inactive conformations giving rise to growth-factor-independent kinase activation.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the manuscript.

claim: Mutations on different exons of the kinase domain affect the equilibrium between active and inactive conformations giving rise to growth-factor-independent kinase activation.
source: Although the activation of EGFR in normal cells is primarily driven by growth-factor-binding-induced dimerization, mutations on different exons of the kinase domain of the receptor have been found to affect the equilibrium between its active and inactive conformations giving rise to growth-factor-independent kinase activation.
evidence: This is supported by citations and experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: EGFR regulates cell proliferation and differentiation by phosphorylating downstream signaling proteins.
source: The epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is a cell surface receptor, which regulates cell proliferation and differentiation by phosphorylating downstream signaling proteins (Sigismund et al., 2018; Wee and Wang, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Genetic mutations that lead to uncontrolled activation of EGFR have been associated with cancer development.
source: Its physiological activity is tightly regulated and genetic mutations that lead to its uncontrolled activation have been associated with cancer development (Sharma et al., 2007; Sigismund et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Acquired somatic DNA alterations on the gene which encodes EGFR are found in 14–32% of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cases.
source: Indeed, acquired somatic DNA alterations on the gene which encodes EGFR are found in 14–32% of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cases (Collisson et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2016) and are correlated with adverse prognosis (Hirsch et al., 2003; Sharma et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: EGFR mutations are correlated with adverse prognosis in NSCLC.
source: Indeed, acquired somatic DNA alterations on the gene which encodes EGFR are found in 14–32% of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cases (Collisson et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2016) and are correlated with adverse prognosis (Hirsch et al., 2003; Sharma et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: EGFR in-frame deletions in exon 19 are the most prevalent of EGFR kinase domain mutations accounting for 45% of EGFR mutations in NSCLC.
source: EGFR in-frame deletions in exon 19 are the most prevalent of EGFR kinase domain mutations accounting for 45% of EGFR mutations in NSCLC, followed by the L858R missense mutation in exon 21, which accounts for approximately 40–45% of EGFR kinase domain mutations (Sharma et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The L858R missense mutation in exon 21 accounts for approximately 40–45% of EGFR kinase domain mutations.
source: EGFR in-frame deletions in exon 19 are the most prevalent of EGFR kinase domain mutations accounting for 45% of EGFR mutations in NSCLC, followed by the L858R missense mutation in exon 21, which accounts for approximately 40–45% of EGFR kinase domain mutations (Sharma et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Exon 20 insertions (Ex20Ins) collectively account for the third most common category of EGFR mutations found in NSCLC and are detected in 4–10% of the cases.
source: Exon 20 insertions (Ex20Ins) collectively account for the third most common category of EGFR mutations found in NSCLC and are detected in 4–10% of the cases (Arcila et al., 2013; Yasuda et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: β3-αC ΔELREA, L858R, A763-Y764insFQEA, and D770-N771insNPG mutated EGFR proteins are oncogenic in both cell cultures and transgenic mouse models.
source: Consistent with their purported role in the etiology of NSCLC, recent studies have shown that β3-αC ΔELREA, L858R, A763-Y764insFQEA, and D770-N771insNPG mutated EGFR proteins are oncogenic in both cell cultures and transgenic mouse models (Ji et al., 2006; Politi et al., 2006; Sordella et al., 2004; Xu et al., 2007; Yasuda et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: These mutations increase the kinase activity of EGFR and eliminate the dependence of the cancer mutants on EGF binding for activation.
source: These mutations increase the kinase activity of EGFR and eliminate the dependence of the cancer mutants on EGF binding for activation, leading to stimulation of downstream pro-survival and cell-growth pathways, and consequently conferring oncogenic properties on EGFR.
evidence: This is supported by citations and experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: ΔELREA-EGFR exhibits the highest catalytic activity among the studied mutants (29-fold higher than that for wild-type EGFR).
source: It should be noted though that the different mutations lead to different levels of activation, with ΔELREA-EGFR exhibiting the highest catalytic activity among them (29-fold higher than that for wild-type EGFR) (Gilmer et al., 2008), followed by the L858R (23-fold) (Gilmer et al., 2008), the A763-Y764insFQEA (9-fold) (Yasuda et al., 2013), and lastly the D770-N771insNPG (5-fold) (Yasuda et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published experimental data.

claim: L858R EGFR exhibits 23-fold higher catalytic activity than wild-type EGFR.
source: It should be noted though that the different mutations lead to different levels of activation, with ΔELREA-EGFR exhibiting the highest catalytic activity among them (29-fold higher than that for wild-type EGFR) (Gilmer et al., 2008), followed by the L858R (23-fold) (Gilmer et al., 2008), the A763-Y764insFQEA (9-fold) (Yasuda et al., 2013), and lastly the D770-N771insNPG (5-fold) (Yasuda et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published experimental data.

claim: A763-Y764insFQEA EGFR exhibits 9-fold higher catalytic activity than wild-type EGFR.
source: It should be noted though that the different mutations lead to different levels of activation, with ΔELREA-EGFR exhibiting the highest catalytic activity among them (29-fold higher than that for wild-type EGFR) (Gilmer et al., 2008), followed by the L858R (23-fold) (Gilmer et al., 2008), the A763-Y764insFQEA (9-fold) (Yasuda et al., 2013), and lastly the D770-N771insNPG (5-fold) (Yasuda et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published experimental data.

claim: D770-N771insNPG EGFR exhibits 5-fold higher catalytic activity than wild-type EGFR.
source: It should be noted though that the different mutations lead to different levels of activation, with ΔELREA-EGFR exhibiting the highest catalytic activity among them (29-fold higher than that for wild-type EGFR) (Gilmer et al., 2008), followed by the L858R (23-fold) (Gilmer et al., 2008), the A763-Y764insFQEA (9-fold) (Yasuda et al., 2013), and lastly the D770-N771insNPG (5-fold) (Yasuda et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published experimental data.

claim: The kinase domain of EGFR consists of a smaller N-terminal lobe (N-lobe) and a larger C-terminal lobe (C-lobe), with the ATP-binding site located between them.
source: Like other eukaryotic protein kinase domains, the kinase domain of EGFR consists of a smaller N-terminal lobe (N-lobe) and a larger C-terminal lobe (C-lobe), with the ATP-binding site located between them.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about kinase domains.

claim: The N-lobe is composed of five β-strands and a helix referred to as αC-helix.
source: The N-lobe is composed of five β-strands and a helix referred to as αC-helix, whereas the C-lobe is predominantly helical.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about kinase domains.

claim: The C-lobe is predominantly helical.
source: The N-lobe is composed of five β-strands and a helix referred to as αC-helix, whereas the C-lobe is predominantly helical.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about kinase domains.

claim: A conserved lysine (K745) binds to the α- and β-phosphates of ATP.
source: Specifically, a conserved lysine (K745) binds to the α- and β-phosphates of ATP, underlying its importance for efficient phosphate transfer (Honegger et al., 1987; Robinson et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: K745 is stabilized and oriented properly for catalysis by a conserved glutamate (E762) on the αC-helix.
source: This lysine is buried deep within the interlobal cleft, where it is stabilized and oriented properly for catalysis by a conserved glutamate (E762) on the αC-helix.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about kinase catalysis.

claim: When K745 and E762 are mutated, the kinase is unable to bind ATP leading to reduced activity.
source: When these two amino acids are mutated, the kinase is unable to bind ATP leading to reduced activity (Honegger et al., 1987; Jura et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published experimental studies.

claim: The aspartate (D855) of the DFG motif participates in the binding of the catalytic ion.
source: The aspartate (D855) of a conserved Asp–Phe–Gly (DFG) motif found at the N-terminal end of the activation loop (A-loop), is also a key regulatory element as it participates in the binding of the catalytic ion.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about kinase catalysis.

claim: The direct contact of the αC-helix with the N-terminal region of the activation loop together with the lysine-glutamate ion pair couple the conformations of the αC-helix and A-loop to ATP binding.
source: The direct contact of the αC-helix with the N-terminal region of the activation loop together with the lysine-glutamate ion pair couple the conformations of the αC-helix and A-loop to ATP binding.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about kinase regulation.

claim: The full length of the A-loop is often unresolved in crystal structures and not visible in NMR spectra, which is indicative of its high flexibility and conformational variability.
source: The full length of the A-loop is often unresolved in crystal structures and not visible in NMR spectra, which is indicative of its high flexibility and conformational variability.
evidence: This is based on established structural knowledge and observations from crystallography and NMR.

claim: Four conformations of the activation loop are seen in available kinase structures: active, Src-like inactive, substrate competitive, and detached.
source: Broadly speaking, four conformations of the activation loop are seen in available kinase structures: active, Src-like inactive, substrate competitive, and detached (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by structural knowledge and reference to a figure showing these conformations.

claim: The active conformation of the activation loop is shared by almost all protein kinases.
source: The active conformation of the activation loop, which includes the formation of a β-strand (β9-strand) with residues of the C-lobe, is shared by almost all protein kinases, whereas its inactive conformations vary among different kinases.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about kinases.

claim: The Src-like inactive conformation is common in many kinases, including Src, Abl, CDK2, and EGFR and involves the formation of a two-turn helix at the N-terminal part of the activation loop.
source: The Src-like inactive conformation, named after the resemblance of the conformation to the inactive conformations of the Src kinase, is common in many kinases, including Src, Abl, CDK2, and EGFR and involves the formation of a two-turn helix at the N-terminal part of the activation loop.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about kinases.

claim: In the detached conformation, the activation loop assumes an extended conformation and the short αEF-helix is detached from the main body of the kinase.
source: In the detached conformation, the activation loop assumes an extended conformation and the short αEF-helix is detached from the main body of the kinase (Shan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The detached conformation is typically seen in kinase dimers in which the activation loop engages in intermolecular interactions, which may underlie trans-autophosphorylation.
source: This conformation is typically seen in kinase dimers in which the activation loop engages in intermolecular interactions, which may underlie trans-autophosphorylation (Pike et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The activation of EGFR is associated with several rearrangements of different structural elements, including that of the αC-helix of the N-lobe of the kinase domain.
source: It has been established that the activation of EGFR is associated with several rearrangements of different structural elements, apart from the ones seen in the activation loop, including that of the αC-helix of the N-lobe of the kinase domain (Endres et al., 2011; Kovacs et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In the active conformation, the αC-helix adopts the αC-in conformation, which is characterized by the full formation of the catalytic spine and the formation of the KE salt bridge between K745 and E762.
source: In the active conformation, the αC-helix adopts the so-called αC-in conformation, which is characterized by the full formation of the so-called catalytic spine and the formation of the functionally important KE salt bridge between K745 and E762.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about kinase activation.

claim: The helix also adopts the αC-out conformation in inactive forms of EGFR, in which the αC-helix is displaced, and the KE salt bridge is broken.
source: The helix also adopts the αC-out conformation in inactive forms of EGFR, in which the αC-helix is displaced, and the KE salt bridge is broken.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about kinase inactivation.

claim: Long-timescale molecular dynamics simulations supported by H/D exchange experiments have identified the presence of a functionally important conformation of EGFR, in which the αC-helix exhibits local disorder (partial unfolding).
source: Long-timescale molecular dynamics simulations supported by H/D exchange experiments have identified the presence of a functionally important conformation of EGFR, in which the αC-helix exhibits local disorder (partial unfolding) (Shan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published computational and experimental studies.

claim: The intrinsically disordered nature of the αC-helix has been postulated to be essential for the regulation of lateral propagation of EGFR signal in the absence of external stimulation through the formation of asymmetric homodimers or higher-order oligomers.
source: This intrinsically disordered nature of the αC-helix has been postulated to be essential for the regulation of lateral propagation of EGFR signal in the absence of external stimulation through the formation of asymmetric homodimers or higher-order oligomers, which is an essential step for the activation of EGFR (Zanetti-Domingues et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Phosphorylation of Y869 has been shown to stabilize the αC-helix, lowering the energy threshold for EGFR multimerization and leading to propagation of the signal.
source: Specifically, phosphorylation of Y869 has been shown to stabilize the αC-helix, and therefore the region that the receiver EGFR monomer binds to, lowering thus the energy threshold for EGFR multimerization and leading to propagation of the signal (Shan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Most Ex20Ins mutations have been shown to render EGFR resistant to most tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs).
source: As most Ex20Ins mutations have been shown to render EGFR resistant to most tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) (Yasuda et al., 2012; Ward et al., 2021), with the exception of the relatively rare A763-Y764insFQEA insertion, we tried to rationalize the behavior of a prototypical Ex20Ins, D770-N771insNPG, and of A763-Y764insFQEA, for which structural and biochemical data is available.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A763-Y764insFQEA insertion is an exception to Ex20Ins resistance to TKIs.
source: As most Ex20Ins mutations have been shown to render EGFR resistant to most tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) (Yasuda et al., 2012; Ward et al., 2021), with the exception of the relatively rare A763-Y764insFQEA insertion, we tried to rationalize the behavior of a prototypical Ex20Ins, D770-N771insNPG, and of A763-Y764insFQEA, for which structural and biochemical data is available.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The unbiased MD simulations of the isolated monomers and the asymmetric homodimers collectively lasted 36 µs for the WT and the mutant forms.
source: The unbiased MD simulations of the isolated monomers and the asymmetric homodimers collectively lasted 36 µs for the WT and the mutant forms (see Materials and methods, Table 1).
evidence: This is data from the simulations performed in this study.

claim: In simulations initiated from the active conformation of the apo, unphosphorylated EGFR monomer, the wild-type (WT) EGFR repeatedly departed from its initial αC-in conformation and transitioned to an αC-out-like conformation within ∼100 ns.
source: In the simulations that we initiated from the active conformation of the apo, unphosphorylated EGFR monomer, the wild-type (WT) EGFR repeatedly departed from its initial αC-in conformation and transitioned to an αC-out-like conformation within ∼100 ns (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) that resembles the conformation seen in the DFG-out inactive state (PDB ID: 2RF9).
evidence: This is data from the MD simulations performed in this study.

claim: Although the K745-E762 salt bridge was broken in WT simulations, the repositioning of the αC-helix was not sufficient for the A-loop to adopt the characteristic two-turn helix that is found in the Src-like inactive conformation.
source: However, although the K745-E762 salt bridge was broken, the repositioning of the αC-helix was not sufficient for the A-loop to adopt the characteristic two-turn helix that is found in the Src-like inactive conformation.
evidence: This is data from the MD simulations performed in this study.

claim: The A-loop remained extended throughout the WT simulations, suggesting the presence of an energy barrier that needs to be crossed for the A-loop to break the β9-strand and form the characteristic two-turn helix.
source: In fact, the A-loop remained extended throughout the simulations, which suggests the presence of an energy barrier that needs to be crossed for the A-loop to break the β9-strand and form the characteristic two-turn helix (Sutto and Gervasio, 2013).
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation data and supported by citation.

claim: Dimerization is important for keeping the αC-helix in the αC-in conformation.
source: This behavior is in line with the known activation mechanism of EGFR according to which dimerization is important for keeping the αC-helix in the αC-in conformation (Shan et al., 2012) and suggests that the presence of ATP and phosphorylation may also be critical for full stabilization of the active conformation.
evidence: This is supported by citation and inference from simulation data.

claim: The presence of ATP and phosphorylation may be critical for full stabilization of the active conformation.
source: This behavior is in line with the known activation mechanism of EGFR according to which dimerization is important for keeping the αC-helix in the αC-in conformation (Shan et al., 2012) and suggests that the presence of ATP and phosphorylation may also be critical for full stabilization of the active conformation.
evidence: This is speculation based on simulation data and established knowledge.

claim: The αC-helix is kept in the αC-in conformation predominately on the receiver monomer in asymmetric WT-EGFR dimer simulations.
source: In particular, we see that the αC-helix is kept in the αC-in conformation predominately on the receiver monomer (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is data from the MD simulations performed in this study.

claim: The αC-helix of the activator monomer is flexible enough to adopt αC-out conformations in asymmetric WT-EGFR dimer simulations.
source: On the contrary, the αC-helix of the activator monomer is flexible enough to adopt αC-out conformations, similar to the ones the αC-helix adopts in the monomeric form of EGFR.
evidence: This is data from the MD simulations performed in this study.

claim: In simulations of the symmetric dimer, the αC-helix of both monomers remains in the αC-out conformations throughout the simulation.
source: Unlike the behavior of the αC-helix that we see in the asymmetric dimer, in the simulations of the symmetric dimer, in which both monomers are found in the Src-like inactive conformation, the αC-helix of both monomers remains in the αC-out conformations throughout the simulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is data from the MD simulations performed in this study.

claim: The free energy landscape reconstructed from multiple replica metadynamics simulations shows three main minima for WT-EGFR.
source: The free energy landscape reconstructed from multiple replica metadynamics simulations shows three main minima.
evidence: This is data from the metadynamics simulations performed in this study.

claim: In the absence of a ligand or phosphorylation, the three main minima for WT-EGFR correspond to inactive-like conformations.
source: As expected, in the absence of a ligand or phosphorylation, these minima for the WT-EGFR correspond to inactive-like conformations (Figure 2).
evidence: This is data from the metadynamics simulations performed in this study.

claim: The deepest free energy minimum for WT-EGFR contains conformations in which the A-loop has adopted a semi-closed conformation that precludes ATP-binding, while the αC-helix is mostly ordered and has adopted the αC-out conformation.
source: Specifically, the ensemble of conformations that corresponds to the deepest free energy minimum – (CV1, CV2) = (0.6, 0.16) – contains conformations in which the A-loop has adopted a semi-closed conformation that precludes the ATP-binding, while the αC-helix is mostly ordered and has adopted the αC-out conformation (Figure 2, basin α1).
evidence: This is data from the metadynamics simulations performed in this study.

claim: In one of the two secondary free energy minima for WT-EGFR, the characteristic two-turn helix on the A-loop of the Src-like inactive conformation is formed and the αC-helix has rotated away from the C-lobe and adopted the αC-out conformation.
source: In one of the two secondary free energy minima - (CV1, CV2) = (1.4, 0.1) — the characteristic two-turn helix on the A-loop of the Src-like inactive conformation is formed and the αC-helix has rotated away from the C-lobe and adopted the αC-out conformation (Figure 2, basin α2).
evidence: This is data from the metadynamics simulations performed in this study.

claim: In the most populated state of basin α2 for WT-EGFR, the N-terminal region of the αC-helix is unfolded.
source: Notably, in the most populated state of this basin, the N-terminal region of the αC-helix is unfolded, in accordance with the predicted partially disordered nature of this region (Shan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is data from the metadynamics simulations and supported by citation.

claim: In the L858R mutant, transient, favorable interactions of R858 with D855 and D837 of the DFG and HRD motifs, respectively, and F723 of the P-loop stabilize the Src-like inactive conformation.
source: However, our unbiased simulation of the monomeric L858R starting from the Src-like inactive conformation showed that transient, favorable interactions of R858 with D855 and D837 of the DFG and HRD motifs, respectively, and F723 of the P-loop (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) stabilize the Src-like inactive conformation.
evidence: This is data from the MD simulations performed in this study.

claim: In unbiased simulations where L858R started from the active conformation, the side chain of R858 interacted mainly with E762 only.
source: On the contrary, in our unbiased simulations where L858R started from the active conformation, the side chain of R858 interacted mainly with E762 only (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is data from the MD simulations performed in this study.

claim: The deepest basin in the free energy landscape of L858R corresponds to an ensemble of conformations that are very close to the active conformation.
source: The free energy landscape (Figure 3) shows that the deepest basin corresponds to an ensemble of conformations that are very close to the active conformation (Figure 3, basin δ1).
evidence: This is data from the metadynamics simulations performed in this study.

claim: In the deepest basin of L858R, the positively charged R858 was surrounded by a cluster of negatively charged residues (E758, E762, D837, and D855).
source: The positively charged R858 was surrounded by a cluster of negatively charged residues (E758, E762, D837, and D855) and in this ensemble, the side chain of R858 fluctuated between two states in which it interacts with either D837 and D855, or E758 and E762.
evidence: This is data from the metadynamics simulations performed in this study.

claim: The interactions of R858 with D837 kept the A-loop in an extended, active-like conformation in L858R.
source: The interactions of R858 with D837 kept the A-loop in an extended, active-like conformation, in which the β9-strand on the A-loop is present.
evidence: This is data from the metadynamics simulations performed in this study.

claim: As a result of the favorable interactions of R858 with E758 and E762, the αC-helix exhibited high secondary structure stability in L858R.
source: At the same time, as a result of the favorable interactions of R858 with E758 and E762, the αC-helix exhibited high secondary structure stability as opposed to the disorder seen in the αC-helix of the wild-type.
evidence: This is data from the metadynamics simulations performed in this study.

claim: The presence of R858 favors the active conformation at the expense of the disordered state that is highly populated in the WT.
source: Overall, the presence of R858 favors the active conformation at the expense of the disordered state that is highly populated in the WT.
evidence: This is an inference from the metadynamics simulation data.

claim: Stabilization of the αC-helix through a mutation like L858R has been shown to promote EGFR dimerization and downstream signaling.
source: Stabilization of the αC-helix through a mutation like L858R has been shown to promote EGFR dimerization and downstream signaling, which explains the activating nature of this mutation (Shan et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Based on the crystal structure of the D770-N771insNPG mutant in the active conformation, it has been postulated that the NPG insertion at the C-terminal end of the αC-helix locks the helix in the αC-in conformation.
source: Based on the crystal structure of the D770-N771insNPG mutant in the active conformation, it has been postulated that the NPG insertion at the C-terminal end of the αC-helix, locks the helix in the αC-in conformation (Yasuda et al., ).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from published literature.

claim: In the crystal structure of D770-N771insNPG, the inserted P772 induces a turn that leads to the formation of a hydrogen bond between the backbone of D770 and the amide of the inserted G773.
source: Proline is a residue found commonly in turns and in the case of the D770-N771insNPG, the inserted P772 induces a turn that leads to the formation of a hydrogen bond between the backbone of D770 and the amide of the inserted G773 in the crystal structure.
evidence: This is data from crystal structure analysis.

claim: The backbone hydrogen bond in D770-N771insNPG orients the side chain of D770 such that it forms a salt bridge with R779.
source: This backbone hydrogen bond orients, in turn, the side chain of D770 such that it forms a salt bridge with R779 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) that is maintained throughout the unbiased simulation initiated from the active conformation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), while the inserted N771 interacts with R837 of the E-helix.
evidence: This is data from crystal structure and MD simulations.

claim: The D770-R779 salt bridge is maintained throughout the unbiased simulation of D770-N771insNPG initiated from the active conformation.
source: This backbone hydrogen bond orients, in turn, the side chain of D770 such that it forms a salt bridge with R779 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) that is maintained throughout the unbiased simulation initiated from the active conformation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), while the inserted N771 interacts with R837 of the E-helix.
evidence: This is data from the MD simulations performed in this study.

claim: The same salt-bridge interaction (D770-R779) is lost after about 300 ns in both replicas of the WT simulations.
source: Interestingly, the same salt-bridge interaction is lost after about 300 ns in both replicas of the WT simulations (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A) and R776 forms a hydrogen bond with the backbone of A767 after (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is data from the MD simulations performed in this study.

claim: The K745-E762 salt bridge breaks almost immediately in D770-N771insNPG simulations starting from the active conformation.
source: Given the different behavior of the mutant and WT, one would expect these interactions to stabilize the αC-in conformation in the mutant, however, the K745-E762 salt bridge breaks almost immediately (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the αC-in conformation in which the mutant is found in the crystal structure is probably ligand-induced rather than mutation-induced.
evidence: This is data from the MD simulations and inference about the mechanism.

claim: The αC-in conformation in which D770-N771insNPG is found in the crystal structure is probably ligand-induced rather than mutation-induced.
source: Given the different behavior of the mutant and WT, one would expect these interactions to stabilize the αC-in conformation in the mutant, however, the K745-E762 salt bridge breaks almost immediately (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the αC-in conformation in which the mutant is found in the crystal structure is probably ligand-induced rather than mutation-induced.
evidence: This is an inference from the MD simulation data.

claim: In PTmetaD simulations of D770-N771insNPG and in the absence of a phosphate group on Y869 or a ligand, the αC-helix adopts the αC-out conformation where the K745-E762 salt bridge is broken, but the A-loop assumes an extended, active-like conformation.
source: In the PTmetaD simulations and in the absence of a phosphate group on Y869 or a ligand, the αC-helix adopts the αC-out conformation where the K745-E762 salt bridge is broken, but the A-loop assumes an extended, active-like conformation.
evidence: This is data from the metadynamics simulations performed in this study.

claim: In all the conformations that correspond to the global minimum of D770-N771insNPG, the A-loop is predominately found in the extended, active-like conformation regardless of the order or position of the αC-helix.
source: In all the conformations that correspond to the global minimum of the reported free energy surface, the A-loop is predominately found in the extended, active-like conformation regardless of the order or position of the αC-helix.
evidence: This is data from the metadynamics simulations performed in this study.

claim: The A-loop is kept in the active conformation through the interaction of E762 with K863 of the nine sheet in D770-N771insNPG.
source: Inspection of the structures in this basin suggests that the A-loop is kept in the active conformation through the interaction of E762 with K863 of the nine sheet.
evidence: This is an inference from structural analysis of simulation data.

claim: The insertion in D770-N771insNPG seems to amplify the N/C-lobe separation.
source: Interestingly, in the unbiased simulations of the mutant, as well as in a relatively populated cluster within the broad basin seen in the PTmetaD simulations, the insertion seems to amplify the N/C-lobe separation.
evidence: This is data from the MD and metadynamics simulations performed in this study.

claim: The same N/C-lobe separation was seen also in the activator kinase in the asymmetric dimer of D770-N771insNPG.
source: The same N/C-lobe separation was seen also in the activator kinase in the asymmetric dimer (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is data from the MD simulations performed in this study.

claim: The EGFR Ex20Ins variant A763-Y764insFQEA was the only EGFR Ex20Ins-harboring cell line inhibited by erlotinib at concentrations less than 0.1 µM when studied in vitro.
source: When studied in vitro, the EGFR Ex20Ins variant A763-Y764insFQEA was the only EGFR Ex20Ins-harboring cell line inhibited by erlotinib at concentrations less than 0.1 µM, while other EGFR Ex20Ins, such as the D770-N771insNPG, had a reduced affinity and sensitivity to EGFR TKIs (Yasuda et al., 2013; Hirano et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published experimental studies.

claim: Other EGFR Ex20Ins, such as the D770-N771insNPG, had a reduced affinity and sensitivity to EGFR TKIs.
source: When studied in vitro, the EGFR Ex20Ins variant A763-Y764insFQEA was the only EGFR Ex20Ins-harboring cell line inhibited by erlotinib at concentrations less than 0.1 µM, while other EGFR Ex20Ins, such as the D770-N771insNPG, had a reduced affinity and sensitivity to EGFR TKIs (Yasuda et al., 2013; Hirano et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published experimental studies.

claim: Mutagenesis studies indicate that the A763-Y764insFQEA insertion extends the αC-helix toward the N-terminal direction while the glutamic acid that is inserted through the mutation assumes the role of E762 in the WT-EGFR.
source: Mutagenesis studies indicate that this insertion extends the αC-helix toward the N-terminal direction while the glutamic acid that is inserted through the mutation assumes the role of E762 in the WT-EGFR (Yasuda et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published experimental studies.

claim: The insertion in A763-Y764insFQEA leads to the replacement of I759 with alanine that has a shorter side chain.
source: The insertion leads to the replacement of I759 with alanine that has a shorter side chain.
evidence: This is structural knowledge based on the mutation.

claim: In simulations of A763-Y764insFQEA initiated from the active conformation, the αC-helix transitioned back to the αC-in conformation several times after it visited the αC-out conformation.
source: On the other hand, in the simulations that we initiated from the active conformation, the A763-Y764insFQEA was the only mutant in which the αC-helix transitioned back to the αC-in conformation several times after it visited the αC-out conformation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is data from the MD simulations performed in this study.

claim: The intrinsic tendency of the A750-N756 segment of the N-terminal of the αC-helix to fold may restrict the conformational flexibility of the αC-helix and favor αC-in conformations in A763-Y764insFQEA.
source: This unique behavior implies that the intrinsic tendency of the A750-N756 segment of the N-terminal of the αC-helix to fold that we see in the simulation may restrict the conformational flexibility of the αC-helix and favor αC-in conformations.
evidence: This is an inference from the MD simulation data.

claim: The deepest minimum in the free energy landscape of A763-Y764insFQEA corresponds to an ensemble where the A-loop samples semi-closed conformations, but the αC-helix is stabilized in an αC-in conformation, where the K745-E762 salt bridge is formed.
source: The deepest minimum in the free energy landscape of A763-Y764insFQEA – (CV1, CV2) = (−0.7, 0.3) – corresponds to an ensemble where the A-loop of the mutant samples semi-closed conformations, but unlike the WT, the αC-helix is stabilized in an αC-in conformation, where the K745-E762 salt bridge is formed (Figure 5, basin γ1).
evidence: This is data from the metadynamics simulations performed in this study.

claim: The activity of A763-Y764insFQEA has been found to be sensitive to Hsp90 inhibitors, suggesting that this mutant is dependent on Hsp90 for stability and downstream-signaling.
source: In the case of the A763-Y764insFQEA, the activity of the mutant has been found to be sensitive to Hsp90 inhibitors, suggesting that this mutant is dependent on Hsp90 for stability and downstream-signaling (Jorge et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published experimental studies.

claim: The biological relevance of the observed elongated states with additional space between the two lobes in A763-Y764insFQEA might be to facilitate the recruitment of the Hsp90 chaperone.
source: As the function of this mutant has been shown to be chaperone-dependent (Jorge et al., 2018), the biological relevance of the observed elongated states with additional space between the two lobes might be to facilitate the recruitment of the Hsp90 chaperone.
evidence: This is speculation based on simulation data and published experimental findings.

claim: In the second main minimum of A763-Y764insFQEA, the mutant samples inactive conformations where the two-turn helix on the A-loop is formed and stabilized by interactions of K860 with the inserted glutamic acid, and the shifted E762 and E758, as well as of interaction of L858 with the inserted F764.
source: In the second main minimum – (CV1, CV2) = (1.4, 0.1) – A763-Y764insFQEA samples inactive conformations where the two-turn helix on the A-loop is formed and stabilized by interactions of K860 with the inserted glutamic acid, and the shifted E762 and E758, as well as of interaction of L858 with the inserted F764 (Figure 5, basin γ2).
evidence: This is data from the metadynamics simulations performed in this study.

claim: The fully active state is populated in A763-Y764insFQEA, albeit there is a small thermodynamic penalty of 1–2 kcal mol−1 with respect to the inactive state.
source: Notably, the fully active state is populated, albeit there is a small thermodynamic penalty of 1–2 kcal mol−1 with respect to the inactive state.
evidence: This is data from the metadynamics simulations performed in this study.

claim: In the apo, monomeric form of A763-Y764insFQEA, the insertion results in an extension of the 3 C loop, which seems to provide structural stability to the αC-helix.
source: In the apo, monomeric form, the insertion results in an extension of the 3 C loop, which was expected to increase the mobility of the αC-helix. Instead, in both the unbiased and PTmetaD simulations that we performed, this extension seems to provide structural stability to the αC-helix.
evidence: This is data from the MD and metadynamics simulations performed in this study.

claim: In both monomers of the asymmetric dimer of A763-Y764insFQEA, the αC-helix is kept predominately in the αC-in conformation.
source: Moreover, looking at the position of the αC-helix in the two monomers of the asymmetric dimer, we see that, unlike the WT, the αC-helix is kept predominately in the αC-in conformation in both monomers (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is data from the MD simulations performed in this study.

claim: EGFR mutants harboring ΔELREA show increased activity, comparable to the activity seen in L858R mutants and much higher than the one seen in the WT.
source: EGFR mutants harboring ΔELREA show increased activity, comparable to the activity seen in L858R mutants and much higher than the one seen in the WT (Foster et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published experimental studies.

claim: Foster et al. showed that the deletion of five amino acids at the 3 C loop is optimal for kinase activation as this deletion is expected to prevent αC-helix from adopting an αC-out conformation.
source: Foster et al. showed that the deletion of five amino acids at the 3 C loop is optimal for kinase activation as this deletion is expected to prevent αC-helix from adopting an αC-out conformation (Foster et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from published literature.

claim: ΔELREA EGFR is still oncogenic even in the absence of asymmetric homodimerization.
source: Moreover, it has been recently shown that ΔELREA EGFR is still oncogenic even in the absence of asymmetric homodimerization (Cho et al., 2013), unlike the wild-type and L858R EGFR, which acquire their oncogenic properties following asymmetric dimerization.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published experimental studies.

claim: Wild-type and L858R EGFR acquire their oncogenic properties following asymmetric dimerization.
source: Moreover, it has been recently shown that ΔELREA EGFR is still oncogenic even in the absence of asymmetric homodimerization (Cho et al., 2013), unlike the wild-type and L858R EGFR, which acquire their oncogenic properties following asymmetric dimerization.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published experimental studies.

claim: Modeling of the ΔELREA deletion in the active conformation suggests that the deletion does not significantly perturb the overall kinase domain.
source: Modeling of the ΔELREA deletion in the active conformation suggests that the deletion does not significantly perturb the overall kinase domain.
evidence: This is an inference from structural modeling performed in this study.

claim: Modeling of the Src-like inactive conformation of ΔELREA suggests that unfolding of the turn at the N-terminal end of the αC-helix is necessary for it to adopt the characteristic αC-out conformation.
source: On the other hand, modeling of the Src-like inactive conformation suggests that unfolding of this turn at the N-terminal end of the αC-helix is necessary for it to adopt the characteristic αC-out conformation.
evidence: This is an inference from structural modeling performed in this study.

claim: Long unbiased molecular dynamics simulations by Shan et al. suggest that the ΔELREA mutation stabilizes the αC-in active conformation relative to the Src-like inactive conformation, but the mutation does not prevent αC-helix from sampling the αC-out conformation.
source: Long unbiased molecular dynamics simulations by Shan et al. suggest that the ΔELREA mutation stabilizes the αC-in active conformation relative to the Src-like inactive conformation, but the mutation does not prevent αC-helix from sampling the αC-out conformation (Shan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published computational studies.

claim: In unbiased simulations of ΔELREA, the αC-out is a stable conformation in terms of the structural integrity of the two-turn helix on the A-loop, the αC-helix and the overall folding of the receptor.
source: In our unbiased simulations, we confirm that the αC-out is a stable conformation in terms of the structural integrity of the two-turn helix on the A-loop, the αC-helix and the overall folding of the receptor.
evidence: This is data from the MD simulations performed in this study.

claim: In one of the deepest free energy minima of ΔELREA, the characteristic two-turn helix on the A-loop of the Src-like inactive conformation is formed, and the αC-helix has shifted to adopt the αC-out conformation.
source: The reconstructed free energy landscape confirms this observation, as the αC-helix is found in the αC-out conformation in one of deepest free energy minima – (CV1, CV2) = (1.4, 0.1) – the characteristic two-turn helix on the A-loop of the Src-like inactive conformation is formed, and the αC-helix has shifted to adopt the αC-out conformation (Figure 6, basin β2).
evidence: This is data from the metadynamics simulations performed in this study.

claim: The deleted L747 in ΔELREA is replaced by P753, and the stability of the Src-like inactive conformation is not compromised despite the deletion.
source: The deleted L747, which on the WT contributes to the stabilization of the two-turn helix through a hydrophobic network between I759, L861, and L858 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), is replaced by P753 (Figure 6, basin β2) and, therefore, the stability of the Src-like inactive conformation is not compromised despite the deletion.
evidence: This is an inference from structural analysis of simulation data.

claim: In the second free energy minimum of ΔELREA, the mutant sampled mainly active-like conformations in which the αC-helix was in the αC-out conformation, but the A-loop assumed extended conformations.
source: In the second free energy minimum – (CV1, CV2) = (1.6, 0.45) – ΔELREA sampled mainly active-like conformations in which the C was again in the αC-out conformation, but the A-loop assumed extended conformations (Figure 6, basin β1) similar to those seen in the unbiased simulations of the active WT-EGFR.
evidence: This is data from the metadynamics simulations performed in this study.

claim: The A-loop in ΔELREA also visited conformations in which the middle section of the A-loop formed a three-turn helix, reminiscent of an extended helix in the A-loop of MPSK1 kinase.
source: Interestingly, the A-loop in this ensemble also visited conformations in which the middle section of the A-loop formed a three-turn helix, reminiscent of an extended helix in the A-loop of MPSK1 kinase (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, PDB ID: 2BUJ).
evidence: This is data from the metadynamics simulations performed in this study.

claim: This helical conformation of the activation loop in ΔELREA might be involved in the phosphorylation of Y869.
source: This helical conformation of the activation loop might be involved in the phosphorylation of Y869.
evidence: This is speculation based on structural analysis of simulation data.

claim: Simulations of ΔELREA-EGFR in the asymmetric dimer do not show any significant alteration on the interface of the mutant dimer with respect to the WT, apart from the marginal stabilization of the inter-monomeric salt bridges K944-E962 and K752-E958.
source: Our simulations of the ΔELREA-EGFR in the asymmetric dimer do not show any significant alteration on the interface of the mutant dimer with respect to the WT, apart from the marginal stabilization of the inter-monomeric salt bridges K944-E962 and K752-E958 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is data from the MD simulations performed in this study.

claim: Suppression of the intrinsic disorder of the αC-helix of the monomeric ΔELREA mutant should promote the formation of active asymmetric dimers.
source: We anticipate, however, that suppression of the intrinsic disorder of the αC-helix of the monomeric mutant that we see in all of the explored conformations during the PTmetaD simulations should promote the formation of active asymmetric dimers.
evidence: This is speculation based on simulation data and established knowledge.

claim: The amplification of the lobe separation observed in D770-N771insNPG could explain the low sensitivity of D770-N771insNPG-EGFR to TKIs, as this motion is expected to affect the residence time of the TKIs in the binding site.
source: According to our simulations, we reason that the amplification of the lobe separation that we observed in both the unbiased and PTmetaD simulations could explain the low sensitivity of D770-N771insNPG-EGFR to TKIs, as this motion is expected to affect the residence time of the TKIs in the binding site.
evidence: This is speculation based on simulation data.

claim: BDTX-189 exhibited potent tumor growth inhibition and tumor regression in preclinical models.
source: Interestingly, BDTX-189, a recently developed inhibitor that targets Ex20Ins mutations, exhibited potent tumor growth inhibition and tumor regression in preclinical models (Hamilton et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published experimental studies.

claim: The scaffold of BDTX-189 is similar to that of the lapatinib analogue neratinib, which suggests that BDTX-189 probably binds αC-out conformations.
source: The scaffold of BDTX-189 is similar to that of the lapatinib analogue neratinib, which suggests that BDTX-189 probably binds αC-out conformations in accordance with the low energy of such states on the free energy landscape of D770-N771insNPG.
evidence: This is inference based on structural similarity and simulation data.

claim: The mutation in D770-N771insNPG possibly decouples the N/C-lobe motions and subsequently the coupling between the αC-helix and the A-loop and makes the transition to the inactive conformation less favorable.
source: It is possible that the mutation decouples the N/C-lobe motions and subsequently the coupling between the αC-helix and the A-loop –a coupling that is important for the transition from the active to the inactive state (Huse and Kuriyan, 2002) – and makes the transition to the inactive conformation less favorable.
evidence: This is speculation based on simulation data and established knowledge.

claim: Recent data show that the A763-Y764insFQEA insertion has greater sensitivity to agents such as gefitinib, erlotinib, and osimertinib.
source: Unlike the majority of EGFR Ex20Ins (including the relatively rare D770-N771insNPG), which appear to be relatively insensitive to early EGFR TKI's, recent data show that the A763-Y764insFQEA insertion has greater sensitivity to agents such as gefitinib, erlotinib, and osimertinib (Yasuda et al., 2013; Floc'h et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published experimental studies.

claim: The most stable conformation of the apo A763-Y764insFQEA corresponds to an αC-in conformation in which the A-loop is not fully extended as seen in the active conformation.
source: Our simulations show that the most stable conformation of the apo A763-Y764insFQEA corresponds to an αC-in conformation in which, however, the A-loop is not fully extended as seen in the active conformation.
evidence: This is data from the metadynamics simulations performed in this study.

claim: The fully active conformation appears as a relatively low energy secondary minimum in the FES of the A763-Y764insFQEA.
source: Interestingly, the fully active conformation that is not favorable in the apo WT-EGFR, appears as a relatively low energy secondary minimum in the FES of the A763-Y764insFQEA.
evidence: This is data from the metadynamics simulations performed in this study.

claim: The A763-Y764insFQEA mutation is anticipated to promote the formation of asymmetric dimers.
source: What is more, after simulation of a homology model of the mutation in the asymmetric dimer, we anticipate the mutation to also promote the formation of such dimers, which would explain the higher activity of A763-Y764insFQEA-EGFR compared to D770-N771insNPG-EGFR.
evidence: This is inference from simulation data.

claim: The introduced F760 of A763-Y764insFQEA is accommodated in the hydrophobic cleft formed by V952, M949, and K953.
source: Specifically, the introduced F760 of A763-Y764insFQEA is accommodated in the hydrophobic cleft formed by V952, M949, and K953, while K757 of the receiver kinase in the WT is replaced by D761 in the A763-Y764insFQEA, which can interact with K953 of the activator kinase (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is data from structural analysis of simulation data.

claim: K757 of the receiver kinase in the WT is replaced by D761 in the A763-Y764insFQEA, which can interact with K953 of the activator kinase.
source: Specifically, the introduced F760 of A763-Y764insFQEA is accommodated in the hydrophobic cleft formed by V952, M949, and K953, while K757 of the receiver kinase in the WT is replaced by D761 in the A763-Y764insFQEA, which can interact with K953 of the activator kinase (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is data from structural analysis of simulation data.

claim: The conformational ensembles from the PTmetaD simulations of the EGFR Ex20Ins with the more extended conformations that lead to a more open active site can be used to identify novel inhibitors with increased selectivity against the mutant EGFR.
source: We believe that the conformational ensembles from the PTmetaD simulations of the EGFR Ex20Ins with the more extended conformations that lead to a more open active site can be used to identify novel inhibitors with increased selectivity against the mutant EGFR.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications of the simulation data.

claim: Targeting the L858R-EGFR with αC-out inhibitors, like lapatinib, would lead to steric clashes that are not present in the pocket of an Ex20Ins EGFR like A763-Y764insFQEA.
source: For example, we can already see that targeting the L858R-EGFR with αC-out inhibitors, like lapatinib, would lead to steric clashes that are not present in the pocket of an Ex20Ins EGFR like A763-Y764insFQEA, while inhibitors like gefitinib can be accommodated better in the tighter pocket of L858R (Figure 7—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is inference from structural analysis of simulation data.

claim: Inhibitors like gefitinib can be accommodated better in the tighter pocket of L858R.
source: For example, we can already see that targeting the L858R-EGFR with αC-out inhibitors, like lapatinib, would lead to steric clashes that are not present in the pocket of an Ex20Ins EGFR like A763-Y764insFQEA, while inhibitors like gefitinib can be accommodated better in the tighter pocket of L858R (Figure 7—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is inference from structural analysis of simulation data.

claim: The absence of intrinsically disordered conformations in the free energy landscape of ΔELREA could explain the decreased sensitivity of ΔELREA-EGFR to lapatinib.
source: It is, thus, tempting to speculate that the absence of such intrinsically disordered conformations in the free energy landscape of ΔELREA could explain the decreased sensitivity of ΔELREA-EGFR to lapatinib.
evidence: This is speculation based on simulation data and established knowledge.

claim: The a99SB-disp force field has been shown to be able to reproduce reliably the dynamics of both well-folded and partially unfolded domains.
source: The chosen force field has been shown to be able to reproduce reliably the dynamics of both well-folded and partially unfolded domains (Robustelli et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.
